newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Govt reviews $94m decision to rehouse cabinet.
newsitem.headline: NZ Govt reviews $94m decision to rehouse cabinet.

text.p: The government is reviewing its decision to spend NZ$94 million on a new building to house cabinet ministers, a government source said on Tuesday.

Heated public debate over the amount MPs spend on themselves, combined with a tight fiscal approach in the run-up to June's Budget, has made some MPs nervous of how the public might view spending on a new office, the source told Reuters.
The source said a recent furore played out in the media over the standard of maintenance in a state-owned block of flats was also a factor in the review.

A spokesman for Prime Minister Jim Bolger told Reuters later, "The Treasury ministers will be reviewing (the project) in light of the budget. However, there is every indication the building will proceed,"

Contractors last weekend demolished an existing building to make way for the new cabinet complex and plans are well advanced to relocate Radio New Zealand from its Broadcasting House office, adjacent to parliament, which will also be demolished.
The building planned for the site, which would house 26 ministers and their support staff, has the strong support of Foreign Affairs and Trade Minister Don McKinnon.
But the three top fiscal ministers -- Treasurer Winston Peters, Finance Minister Bill Birch and Associate Treasurer Tuariki John Delamere -- have started dragging their heels.
"Cabinet gave the green light a week ago, but the three treasury ministers are opposed to the spending," the source told Reuters.
The trio are currently finalising the numbers for June's Budget which will see $950 million in new spending in the 1997/98 year.

The ministers are paring back planned spending of $1.2 billion, agreed as part of the coalition deal between the conservative National Party and nationalist New Zealand First in December, to accommodate Budget measures within the lower cap.

The source said scrapping the $94 million allocated for the new building over the next three years could be a useful public symbol of politicians' willingness to show restraint at a time when spending in social policy areas is under tight control.

Plans for the new building come on top of $168 million just spent refurbishing the historical parliament buildings and a planned $20 million upgrade of the executive wing, known as the Beehive, where most ministers now have their offices.
